newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deadlock in German tax talks threatens reform.
newsitem.headline: Deadlock in German tax talks threatens reform.

text.p: Germany's plan to slash income and company taxes, dubbed the 'reform of the century' by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government, has no chance of becoming law soon, the government and opposition said on Tuesday.

Negotiators on both sides said working groups seeking a last-chance deal in parliament's mediation process failed to agree on even a watered-down version of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax reform project.

Neither were Kohl's centre-right coalition and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) able to agree on SPD proposals to cut high social insurance charges to help fight record post-war unemployment of over four million.
Talks continued on Tuesday afternoon to try to end a two-year row over scrapping a capital trading tax on companies. But even there, hopes of a deal were muted.

"The talks have become increasingly difficult," government tax negotiator Hans-Peter Repnik, a member of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), told a news briefing during a lunchtime break in the negotiations.
"It has become clear the SPD has adopted a position which makes an agreement on the tax reform impossible," he added.
Waigel's original model to slice a net 30 billion marks off the national tax bill was thrown out of the Bundesrat upper house of parliament by the SPD majority in early July.

Coalition negotiators came back with a proposal to reduce taxes by 15 billion marks -- but even that was not enough to satisfy the SPD, which supports revenue-neutral measures which would lighten employers' payroll costs.

SPD chief whip Peter Struck told reporters his party would not agree to a tax reform "a la Kohl and Waigel" in mediation -- the last chance under the German parliamentary process to salvage a compromise.
He said the government had blocked SPD proposals to knock one percentage point each off pensions and unemployment insurance charges this autumn to boost job creation and consumer demand.
"Clearly, the coalition doesn't want to cut insurance charges as soon as October," Struck told reporters before talks resumed on Tuesday afternoon.
Struck said the chances of reaching a deal to scrap the corporate capital trading tax -- levied irrespective of whether a firm makes a profit -- were "not too bad".

Repnik also said he hoped a deal here was possible. Failure to agree would mean the introduction of the tax in depressed eastern Germany. The only remaining issue is how to compensate municipal governments for lost revenues.

Parliament's mediation committee, on which the SPD has a majority, will meet formally on Wednesday to put its recommendations to the Bundestag lower house, which will meet in special session in a week's time.

There, the two sides are likely to trade the blame for what appears to be a serious breakdown in Germany's consensus-based politics, opening the way for an epic campaign ahead of general elections in September 1998.
Repnik said the government might invoke parliamentary mediation a second time to force the SPD to shoulder its political responsibility to the German nation.
But, one coalition source said, failure at the second attempt at mediation would not deflect the government from its goal of reforming the tax system.
"For us, the tax reform remains the main point for creating jobs and investment, and, if necessary, we will fight the election campaign on it," the source said.
